description_full: The New York Times Company, together with its subsidiaries, creates, collects, and distributes news and information worldwide. It operates through two segments, The New York Times Group and The Athletic. It offers The New York Times (The Times) through company's mobile application, website, printed newspaper, and associated content, such as podcast. The company offers The Athletic, a sports media product; Cooking, a recipe product; Games, a puzzle games product; and Audio, an audio product. In addition, the company offers a portfolio of advertising products and services to advertisers, such as luxury goods, technology, and financial companies, to promote products, services or brands on digital platforms in the form of display ads, audio and video, in print in the form of column-inch ads, and at live events; and Wirecutter, a product review and recommendation product. Further, the company licenses content to digital aggregators in the business, professional, academic and library markets, and third-party digital platforms; articles, graphics, and photographs, including newspapers, magazines, and websites; and for use in television, films, and books, as well as provide rights to reprint articles, and create and sell new digests. Additionally, the company engages in commercial printing and distribution for third parties; and operates the NYTimes.com website. The company was founded in 1851 and is headquartered in New York, New York.

financial_summary: New York Times Company (The) is a large-cap communication services business with a $11.6B market cap on $2.8B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +7% over the past three years and +6% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 20% against a 8% cost of capital — a 12-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $551M in free cash flow — roughly 19 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.70× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 2.4% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 11% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.

sector_headwinds.text: Low reinvestment-driven growth suggests the compounding engine has stalled
Fragmented industry with below-average profit capture — no moat to protect margins
Carries a 93% premium to sector median EV/EBITDA (confirmed by 1 other valuation measure)
Elevated short interest (11.9% of float) — sophisticated money is betting the other way
Advertising-cycle exposure and content/regulatory risk — a single platform policy shift or ad-spend contraction cascades through the P&L quickly.
Cord-cutting acceleration and audience fragmentation — legacy distribution bundles unravel faster than subscription revenue can replace them.
AI-generated content commoditisation — as creation costs collapse toward zero, content libraries lose pricing power and differentiation narrows.

sector_tailwinds: Altman Z comfortably in the safe zone — a fortress balance sheet on this measure
13 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment

sect: Its 15% operating margin runs 7pp above the Communication Services median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.74x).
It accounts for 0.1% of sector revenue and 0.1% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+3.8% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.06 across 171 companies in the universe; the top four hold 36% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are roughly flat over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 16% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 32% and a beta of 0.64, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y -0.32 vs 5y 0.55), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $135.0M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 28% in the 2020 crash, 42% in the 2022 bear market and 83% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $59.58 (margin of safety -22%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 33%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $47.22 to $77.31 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Communication Services peers: P/E 29.1 vs 15.4, EV/EBITDA 18.6 vs 9.9 and P/FCF 21.1 vs 11.1 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 5% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 4.7% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The 9 covering analysts target $77.00 on average, 6% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 20% clears the cost of capital of 8.0% by 12pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.33).
It converts 19% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.70x.
ROE of 17% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.5x equity multiplier).
It spends 9.4% of revenue on R&D and 2.6% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $642.2M.
Its debt comes due soon (maturity wall about 0.5 years out), so refinancing terms matter.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 7.0% over 3 years, 9.6% over 5 years and 6.0% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 15.9% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.00, a backlog worth 5% of annual revenue and deferred revenue up 11%.
Capex runs only 0.4x depreciation (1.2% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 26, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own 11.4%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 96%.
It returns 2.4% a year to shareholders (1.4% in buybacks and 1.3% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 13 consecutive years, raising it 23.5% a year over the last five.
Short interest is elevated at 11.9% of the float, 9.3 days to cover.
people: With about 6,000 employees, each generates about $471K of revenue, 0.8x the Communication Services median.
That works out to $92K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $3.0M (6x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
